title: Two things
hookLine: Kant: the starry heavens above and the moral law within fill the mind with awe

cards: Two directions. Up, where the stars are. And in, where a sense of duty says: this must be done.
Immanuel Kant spent a whole book on duty and reason, argued step by careful step. Then, in its conclusion, he stops arguing and writes something closer to a confession.
Two things, he says, fill the mind with admiration and awe, and the feeling grows the more often and the more steadily we think about them. The starry heavens above. And the moral law within.

teach.b: First, the pairing. Stars are easy to stand in awe of. Kant sets beside them something that doesn't shine at all: the sense, inside a person, that some things must be done and some must not, whatever they cost.
He says he doesn't have to hunt for either one as if it were hidden in darkness. He sees them both in front of him, and ties them straight to the awareness of his own existence. Second, the sky.

The view of a countless crowd of worlds, Kant says, seems to wipe out his importance, as a creature of matter who must give that matter back to the planet he stands on. Pascal felt that smallness as fear.
Kant names it plainly and doesn't look away. Third, the law within. Here the arithmetic flips.

teach.h: THE STARS MAKE A PERSON SMALL
teach.b: The same person who shrinks under the stars is raised up by the moral law, given a worth that doesn't depend on size, or the body, or the world of things.

teach.h: THE LAW WITHIN MAKES A PERSON LARGE

teach.b: A view seen every day can wear thin.
Kant claims the opposite for these two: the oftener and the more steadily you reflect, the more they fill the mind.
Some readers hear in that a practice, not just a feeling: looking up, and looking in, every day, and finding they don't wear out.

how: Readers of Kant often meet this passage on its own, and some people who keep a reflective practice pair a look at the night sky with an evening review of their own conduct.

s: Kant says the awe fades the more you think about these two things
he says it grows, the oftener and more steadily we reflect on them.
Kant says he doesn't have to search for them as if hidden in darkness
he says he sees them before him and ties them to the awareness of his own existence.
in the passage, the sky and the law within do the same thing to a person
the sky seems to shrink a person's importance; the law within raises a person's worth.

games.q: you're Kant, finishing a long, careful book about duty and reason. how do you end it?
o: with two things that fill the mind with awe: the stars above and the moral law within.
with a warning not to look at the sky.
games.why: in the conclusion he sets the starry heavens and the moral law side by side, and says the awe they bring keeps growing.

practice: Look up first, at the sky through a window or outside, or at whatever is above you, and let it be bigger than you are.

Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward: is there one thing you already know is right to do, a call owed, a truth to tell, a kindness put off? Don't argue with it; just look at it, the way you looked at the sky.

wordCard.voice: Two things. Kant's pair: the starry heavens above, the moral law within, and the awe that grows the longer you look at them. Today's word.

orig.note: German, Kant's own words: the starry heaven above me.

carryVoice: Your line: above and within. The stars shrink you, and the law within lifts you back up. Rest well.
